q: Why do traditional fully connected networks cope poorly with images?
options: They do not use local groups of neighbouring pixels that form shapes
They cannot apply a nonlinear function to the outputs of their neurons
They cannot be trained using backpropagation at all
They only accept grayscale images with a single channel
explain: The meaning of an image sits in groups of neighbouring pixels, and a fully connected network does not use that local structure. It can still use nonlinear functions and backpropagation, so those options fail.

q: A kernel is moved across an image with a stride of 2 instead of 1. What is the effect?
options: The kernel doubles in size and covers more of the image
The border of the image is filled with zeros first
Each kernel weight is doubled, so the detected features get stronger
The kernel moves two positions per step, so the output is smaller
explain: Stride is the amount the kernel shifts over the input. A bigger shift means fewer positions are visited. Filling the border with zeros describes padding, not stride.

q: Why is padding added around the border of an image before convolution?
options: To enlarge the kernel so it can detect bigger shapes
To convert a colour image with three channels into a single channel image
To handle edge pixels, which the kernel would otherwise cover less
To increase the stride so the kernel moves faster
explain: A sliding kernel treats pixels at the edges differently from the rest, so a border is added. Padding does not change the kernel size, the number of channels or the stride.

q: How does dropout reduce overfitting during training?
options: It permanently deletes the weakest neurons after the first pass
It normalises each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini batch
It reduces the spatial size of the feature maps in each layer
It randomly ignores some layer outputs, so the layer differs on each pass
explain: Dropout is a regularisation technique that randomly drops outputs during training, so the network cannot rely on memorising everything. The dropped outputs are not removed for good.

q: Compare max pooling and average pooling and explain why a CNN uses pooling.
model: A pooling layer reduces the spatial size of the convolved features, which lowers the computing power needed. It also extracts dominant features that do not depend much on position or rotation, which keeps training effective. Max pooling returns the largest value in the patch covered by the kernel. Average pooling returns the mean of all values in that patch. Max pooling keeps the strongest response while average pooling gives a smoother summary.
points: Pooling reduces spatial size and computation
It keeps dominant features that are position and rotation invariant
Max pooling returns the maximum value in the patch
Average pooling returns the mean of the patch

q: Explain what overfitting is and how a dropout layer helps to prevent it.
model: Overfitting happens when the error on the training set is very small but the error on new data is large. The network has memorised the training examples and has not learned to generalise. Dropout is a simple regularisation technique. During training it randomly ignores some layer outputs, so the layer looks different from one pass to the next. This stops the network relying on memorising the whole training set.
points: Overfitting means tiny training error but large error on new data
The network has memorised rather than generalised
It randomly ignores some layer outputs during training

q: Describe the main components of a convolutional neural network and their functions. Explain how CNNs differ from ordinary feedforward networks in processing images.
model: A convolutional layer slides small filters, or kernels, over the image to produce feature maps that detect patterns such as edges and textures. An activation function such as ReLU adds nonlinearity. A pooling layer, for example max pooling, reduces the size of the feature maps and keeps the strongest responses. Batch normalisation normalises feature maps across the mini-batch to speed up training. A dropout layer randomly drops neurons during training to reduce overfitting. Fully connected layers at the end combine the features and give the class output. An ordinary feedforward network is a good classifier but poor at extracting features, and does not scale well to images. It flattens the image and connects every pixel to every neuron, which needs very many weights and loses the spatial layout. A CNN shares the same filter weights across the image and keeps the spatial structure, so it exploits local features, the relationships between neighbouring pixels, with filters that are learned in training.
points: Convolutional layers use filters to make feature maps
Pooling reduces the size of the feature maps
Fully connected layers give the final classification
Feedforward networks flatten the image and need many weights
CNNs exploit local features with learned filters and scale better to images

q: What is the output size of a valid convolution on a 32 x 32 input with a 3 x 3 kernel, stride 1 and no padding?
explain: Output size is (input - kernel) / stride + 1 = (32 - 3) / 1 + 1 = 30 on each side.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 14

q: What is the output of a 2 x 2 max pooling operation on the values [2, 7; 5, 3]?
explain: Max pooling keeps the largest value in the window, which is 7. 4.25 would be average pooling.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 15

q: Which best describes the main function of batch normalisation in a neural network?
options: Eliminating the need for a loss function
Normalising intermediate activations using batch statistics and learned scaling and shifting
Removing all negative activation values
Reducing the number of output classes
explain: Batch normalisation subtracts the mini-batch mean and divides by its standard deviation, then applies a learned scale and shift. Removing negative values is what ReLU does.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 16
